EXECUTIVE SUMMARY
This Report reviews the performance of Uganda's Electricity Supply Industry (ESI) in
2024 across the value chain, generation, transmission, distribution, import, and
export, against established targets and indicators. Industry performance was
shaped by macroeconomic trends such as exchange rates and inflation,
alongside government initiatives like the free connection policy and tariff reforms.
Electricity remains central to Uganda's socio-economic transformation, with
national targets to raise access from 53.4% in 2024 to 70% by 2030, expand clean
cooking access from 25% to 50%, and increase per capita consumption from 218
kWh to 1,090 kWh (NDP IV 2025/26–2029/30). In March 2024, the Ministry of Energy
and Mineral Development, supported by the World Bank, launched the Electricity
Access Scale-up Project (EASP), aiming to connect 1.5 million households,
including refugee and host communities, within five years.
To address affordability, the government has continued implementing the hybrid
customer connection scheme introduced in 2022. By December 2024, this initiative,
supported by ERA and development partners, had enabled 42,487 new
connections in Umeme and UEDCL territories by reducing upfront costs through
shared financing.
The Report thus details generation, transmission, and distribution performance on
both main grid and off-grid systems, and provides projections for the ESI’s
continued role in driving Uganda’s energy access, industrialization, and inclusive
growth.

2 ELECTRICITY TRANSMISSION
Until recently, Uganda Electricity Transmission Company Limited (UETCL) has been
the sole buyer of electricity in Uganda. UETCL holds four licenses: Bulk Power Supply,
Import and Export of Electricity, System Operation, and High Voltage Transmission
Grid. However, the Electricity (Amendment) Act, 2022 restructured this
arrangement, introducing opportunities for Independent Power Transmission and
Direct Purchases by eligible customers. Since then, several companies have
expressed interest in participating in transforming Uganda’s market into a Modified
Single-Buyer Model. UETCL’s energy purchases continue to be demand-driven. This
Section presents Uganda’s 2024 peak demand, UETCL’s energy purchases, and
corresponding sales.

Uganda’s annual peak electricity demand, including both domestic consumption
and exports, was recorded in December 2024 at 1,118 MW, reflecting a 13%
increase from the 988 MW registered in December 2023.

2.5.2 UETCL Energy Sales by Time-of-Use (ToU)
UETCL bills electricity distributors based on a Time-of-Use (ToU) Energy Charge
structure. The Electricity Regulatory Authority (ERA) defines the ToU periods, which
may be revised periodically in response to changes in the national load profile.
Currently, three distinct Time-of-Use periods are in effect:
• Peak: 18:00 to 23:00 (5 hours)
• Shoulder: 05:00 to 18:00 (13 hours)
• Off-Peak: 23:00 to 05:00 (6 hours)
Over the past five years, the majority of UETCL’s energy sales have occurred during
the Shoulder period, accounting for more than 50% of total sales. Sales during the
Off-Peak and Peak periods have averaged 20% and 27%, respectively.
In 2023, this distribution remained consistent, with Shoulder sales comprising 52% of
total energy sold, while Peak and Off-Peak sales accounted for 28% and 20%,

3 ELECTRICITY DISTRIBUTION
By the end of 2024, four primary utilities were carrying out electricity distribution on
Uganda's National Grid: Umeme Limited, Uganda Electricity Distribution Company
Limited (UEDCL), West Nile Rural Electricity Company (WENRECo), and Kalangala
Infrastructure Services (KIS). This configuration followed the expiry of distribution
licenses for Kilembe Investments Limited (KIL) and Kyegegwa Rural Electricity
Cooperative Society (KRECS).
During the reporting period, both WENRECo and KIS were integrated into the
National Grid. Umeme Limited remained the largest operator, followed by UEDCL.
As of December 2024, UEDCL's operations spanned twelve Service Territories,
namely: Central North Service Territory (CNST), Eastern Service Territory (EST), Mid-
West Service Territory (MWST), North East Service Territory (NEST), North-North West
Service Territory (NNWST), Southern Service Territory (SST), South-West Service
Territory (SWST), North-Western Service Territory (NWST), Rwenzori Service Territory
(RST), North-South Service Territory (NST) – formerly PACMECS, Central Service
Territory (CST) – formerly KRECS and Western Service Territory (WST) – formerly KIL
For the purposes of this report, all electricity distribution utilities other than Umeme
Limited are categorized as Mini-Grids.
3.1 Energy Purchases and Sales by Grid-Connected Distribution Utilities
In 2024, electricity distribution utilities operating on the National Grid purchased a
total of 5,822.8 GWh of energy, reflecting an 11% increase from the 5,251.9 GWh
purchased in 2023. Approximately 16.9% of the energy purchased was lost across
the distribution network. Nonetheless, energy sales to end-users rose by 11% in 2024,
reaching 4,802.6 GWh, up from 4,329.8 GWh in the previous year.
During the reporting period, Umeme Limited remained the dominant electricity
distribution utility, accounting for 4,672.5 GWh of energy sold, representing 97% of
total sales. The remaining 3% was collectively sold by other distribution utilities.
Overall, energy purchases increased by 10.9%, while energy sales grew by 11.7%
in 2024 compared to 2023.
As illustrated in Figure 10, the majority of energy sold on the National Grid (64.9%)
was consumed by industrial customers (Medium, Large, and Extra-large). In
contrast, the lowest consumption category was Street Lighting, which accounted
for only 0.1% of total energy sales.

5 RETAIL TARIFFS
The Electricity Regulatory Authority (ERA) sets tariff rates for distribution licensees in
accordance with Sections 10 and 75 of the Electricity Act, Cap 157. The tariff
methodology applied within Uganda's Electricity Supply Industry is responsive to
macroeconomic dynamics and is reviewed periodically as provided for under the
Tariff Regulations.
Tariff adjustments are informed by several factors, including macroeconomic
indicators and the prevailing energy mix. Key macroeconomic parameters
considered in the tariff review process include the Consumer Price Index (CPI), the
U.S. Dollar Producer Price Index (US PPI), the exchange rate of the Uganda Shilling
(UGX) against the U.S. Dollar, and international fuel prices.
ERA sets Base Tariffs annually, which are subsequently adjusted quarterly to reflect
movements in these parameters relative to the base assumptions. This section
presents the tariff outcomes determined by the Authority for the various licensees
across the respective customer categories.

6.4 Initiatives to Grow Electricity Demand and Improve Access
The Electricity Regulatory Authority (ERA) is implementing several strategic
initiatives aligned with the Third National Development Plan (NDP III) and Vision
2040 to enhance access to electricity and promote the use of clean energy. These
efforts are also guided by the Presidential Directives on reducing the cost of
electricity for manufacturers. As part of these efforts, ERA has introduced specific
interventions aimed at lowering tariffs, including the following:
6.4.1 Electricity Tariffs for Industrial Parks
The President of Uganda issued a directive to support industrial growth and reduce
the end-user cost of electricity for manufacturers. The directive also enhances the
competitiveness of locally produced goods and stimulates electricity demand.
The directive stipulates the following:
(i) The cost of electricity supplied to manufacturers, across all categories
including Extra-Large, Large, Medium, and Commercial, shall be set at US
Cents 5 per kilowatt-hour (kWh).
(ii) Industrial Parks shall receive electricity directly from Government-owned
power stations, namely Karuma, Isimba, Nalubaale, and Kiira, bypassing
Umeme Limited as the distribution utility.
27 | Page

This policy intervention is intended to promote industrialization, reduce production
costs, and accelerate economic transformation.
6.4.2 Implementation of the Declining Block tariff
Beginning with the Tariff Year 2020, the Electricity Regulatory Authority (ERA)
approved the implementation of a declining block tariff structure for Large
Industrial and Extra-Large Industrial customers. Under this structure, energy
consumption is segmented into two categories: consumption billed at the
standard tariff rate, based on the prevailing tariff methodology, and additional
consumption billed at a lower rate, the declining block tariff.
The lower tariff applies to energy consumed beyond the historical periodic
baseline, adjusted to account for a reasonable growth trend in consumption. This
incentive is designed to encourage increased industrial productivity and efficiency
by offering reduced rates for incremental usage.
ERA continues to monitor the implementation of this initiative. Following a
comprehensive assessment, 266 companies qualified to benefit from the declining
block tariff. A review conducted between 2023 and 2024 revealed that energy
consumption billed under the declining block increased at an annualized rate of
3.3%.
6.4.3 Biomass to Electricity Cooking
The Electricity Regulatory Authority (ERA) launched the "Charcoal-to-Power
Project," a strategic initiative aimed at curbing the use of biomass for cooking and
promoting electricity consumption among households and institutions. This
campaign is part of ERA's broader effort to stimulate electricity demand while
advancing cleaner and more sustainable energy practices.
To support the initiative, ERA approved a pilot cooking tariff of Ush 451.4 per
kilowatt-hour (kWh) for Mulago National Hospital. The pilot, implemented in
collaboration with the United Nations Development Programme (UNDP), is
intended to generate insights that will guide the scale-up of electric cooking
across other public institutions, including hospitals, prisons, and schools.
For domestic and household consumers, ERA approved a Cooking Tariff of Ush 412
per kWh. The tariff design provides a progressive structure whereby, after the first
80 kWh consumed in a given month, the rate drops from the standard Ush 797.3
(applicable in 2024) to Ush 412 for the next 70 kWh units purchased within the same
month.
Ongoing studies and close monitoring of the initiative have revealed a growing
uptake among domestic customers. ERA continues to undertake deliberate

sensitization efforts to raise awareness about the Cooking Tariff and encourage
broader adoption of electricity for cooking purposes.
6.4.4 The Electricity Access Scale-up Project
In February 2024, the Government of Uganda, through the Ministry of Energy and
Mineral Development and with support from the World Bank, officially launched
the Electricity Access Scale-up Project. This ambitious initiative aims to expand
electricity access by connecting approximately 1,500,000 households over a five-
year period, averaging 300,000 new connections annually.
The project is expected to significantly improve national electricity access statistics,
contributing to Uganda's broader goals of inclusive development, enhanced
service delivery, and economic transformation through increased energy access.
6.4.5 Other initiatives to Grow Electricity Demand and Improve Access
a) Implementation frameworks under the Amended Electricity Act are being
fast-tracked to ensure effective regulation and monitoring of sector
operations.
b) The Government of Uganda continues to invest in transmission and
distribution infrastructure with the objective of minimizing tariff impacts on
end-users.
c) Efforts are being made to accelerate the development of an independent
power transmission framework. This will enable private sector participation in
transmission infrastructure, helping to address longstanding challenges
related to power evacuation and electricity exports that have persisted over
the past five years.
